procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated January 9, 2018 passed by the High Court of Kerala in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 171 of 2018
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Respondent-Accused No. 2 filed Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 171 of 2018 under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. before the High Court of Kerala, aggrieved by the Order dated December 20, 2017 passed by the Additional Sessions Judge. The High Court reversed the Order of the Additional Sessions Judge by an unreasoned Order dated January 1, 2018, and allowed Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 171 of 2018. It directed that the cross-examination of CWs 1 to 4 be adjourned till after the examination-in-chief of CW 5.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of Kerala, aggrieved by the Order dated January 1, 2018 passed by the High Court, filed Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No. 4652 of 2018 before the Supreme Court, which was converted to Criminal Appeal No. 1321 of 2018. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court's order, restoring the Additional Sessions Judge's original order.

directions: The impugned Order dated January 9, 2018 passed by the High Court of Kerala in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 171 of 2018 is set aside.
The Order dated December 20, 2017 passed by the Additional Sessions Judge dismissing the Application filed on behalf of the Respondent-Accused No. 2 stands restored.
The observations made hereinabove will, however, have no bearing on the merits of the case during the course of trial.

issue.issue_text: Whether the exercise of discretion under Section 231(2) of the Cr.P.C. by the Additional Sessions Judge was valid and legally sustainable.

facts: After the examination-in-chief of a prosecution witness (CW-1), the accused (Respondent-Accused No. 2) filed an application under Section 231(2) of the Cr.P.C.
The application sought to postpone the cross-examination of CW-1 and other witnesses (CWs 2 to 5) until after the examination-in-chief of all of them was completed.
The Additional Sessions Judge dismissed this application, stating that deferring cross-examination is not an ordinary practice and that no specific reason was provided by the accused.
law: Section 231(2) of the Cr.P.C. confers a discretion, not a right, on a judge to defer the cross-examination of a witness.
The party seeking deferral must provide sufficient reasons; it cannot be asserted as a matter of right.
The exercise of this discretion is not based on a 'straitjacket formula' but must be decided on a case-to-case basis.
The guiding principle for the judge is to ascertain whether dismissing the application would cause prejudice to the party seeking deferral.
A balance must be struck between the rights of the accused and the prosecution's prerogative to lead evidence.
Factors such as the possibility of undue influence or threats to witnesses must be considered, especially when the accused are influential.
application: The Supreme Court noted that in this specific case, the accused (No. 2 and No. 7) were highly influential political leaders.
This created a significant possibility of undue influence and intimidation of witnesses if their cross-examination was postponed.
The Court determined that the trial court correctly balanced the rights of the accused against the risk of witness intimidation.
The accused's argument that their defence would be revealed was not considered a sufficient reason to justify the deferral in these circumstances.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Additional Sessions Judge's decision to dismiss the application was a valid and legally sustainable exercise of discretion. The Court held that the trial judge was right to deny the deferral, given the potential for the influential accused to intimidate or influence witnesses. Therefore, the order of the Additional Sessions Judge was restored.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the exercise of discretion under Section 231(2) of the Cr.P.C. by the Additional Sessions Judge was valid and legally sustainable.
appellant_arguments: The respondent-accused's request to defer cross-examination was merely a 'bald assertion' that their defence would be prejudiced, without any specific reasons provided.
The High Court erred in reversing the Additional Sessions Judge's order without giving any reasons for the reversal.
Deferring the cross-examination could lead to the possibility of undue influence and intimidation of witnesses, especially since the accused are 'highly influential political leaders'.
The deferral would adversely affect the prosecution's case, as it could cause witnesses to lose memory of the events.
The witnesses in question (CWs 1 to 5) were not deposing on the same subject matter, making a deferred, consolidated cross-examination unnecessary.
respondent_arguments: The defence would be prejudiced if the cross-examination of the first five prosecution witnesses (CWs 1 to 5) was not deferred until after the examination-in-chief of all five was completed.
Conducting the cross-examination immediately after each examination-in-chief would prematurely disclose the defence strategy to the prosecution.

statutes.act_name: Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1955 (Act No. 26 of 1955)

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Once a trial commences, it is expected by law to continue day-to-day until its conclusion. A detailed schedule for recording evidence must be drawn up immediately after the charge is framed, taking into account the court's calendar, the time required by the prosecution to secure its witnesses, and the convenience of the defence counsel. Once prepared, all parties are duty-bound to strictly and scrupulously adhere to this case calendar, and any departure is only permissible when it becomes absolutely necessary.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The exercise of discretion under Section 231(2) of the Cr.P.C. must be based on sufficient reasons provided by the party seeking deferral, and cannot be claimed as a matter of right. The High Court's order was invalid because it failed to provide any reasons for reversing the Additional Sessions Judge's decision, particularly when faced with a significant possibility of witness intimidation by the politically influential accused.
legal_tests_applied: The guiding principle for a Judge under Section 231(2) of the Cr.P.C. is to ascertain whether prejudice would be caused to the party seeking deferral, if the application is dismissed.
The party seeking deferral under Section 231(2) of the Cr.P.C. must give sufficient reasons to invoke the exercise of discretion by the Judge, and deferral cannot be asserted as a matter of right.
The exercise of discretion has to take place on a case-to-case basis.
A judge has the latitude to exercise discretion under Section 231(2) of the Cr.P.C. if sufficient reasons are made out for deviating from the norm.
why_respondent_won: The High Court's impugned order was liable to be set aside because it gave no reasons for reversing the order of the Additional Sessions Judge.

The court accepted the possibility of undue influence and intimidation of witnesses, given that the accused were 'highly influential political leaders', which weighed against deferring cross-examination.

The respondent's request for deferral was not supported by specific reasons, merely a general claim that the defence strategy would be disclosed, which is an insufficient ground for invoking the court's discretion.
policy_considerations: The procedure for criminal trials is intended to ensure speedy disposal of judicial business and minimize inconvenience to witnesses.
Adjournments should not be allowed without the examination of witnesses present in court, except for an unavoidable cause.
The court must consider the possibility of undue influence on witnesses when deciding on procedural matters like the deferral of cross-examination.
